questions.stem:
A 74-year-old man presents after two episodes of light-headedness and one brief loss of consciousness while climbing stairs. He also reports exertional chest tightness over the past 3 months.

BP is 128/84 mmHg, HR 76/min and regular. There is a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotids, with a soft single S2. Carotid upstrokes are delayed. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy.
questions.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Stress testing is contraindicated in symptomatic suspected severe aortic stenosis because of the risk of syncope and sudden death.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Confirms the diagnosis and grades severity (peak velocity, mean gradient, valve area) and assesses LV function.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Useful when arrhythmic syncope is suspected, but the exam points to a structural cause that must be characterized first.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Exertional syncope with a classic murmur is cardiac until proven otherwise; neuroimaging adds little without focal findings.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Evaluates reflex (vasovagal) syncope, which typically does not occur during exertion.

questions.explanation: The triad of exertional syncope, angina, and a late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo murmur with a soft S2 and delayed carotid upstrokes suggests severe aortic stenosis. Transthoracic echocardiography is the initial test to confirm and grade severity. Symptomatic severe AS is an indication for valve replacement (surgical or transcatheter).

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old woman has had dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency for 2 days. She has no fever, flank pain, vaginal discharge or nausea. She is not pregnant and has no drug allergies. She had one similar episode 3 years ago.

Temperature is 36.8°C. There is mild suprapubic tenderness and no costovertebral angle tenderness. Urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites.
questions.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for pyelonephritis or when first-line options cannot be used, given adverse effects and resistance concerns.

options.label: B
options.explanation: High rates of E. coli resistance make amoxicillin a poor empiric choice.

options.label: C
options.explanation: First-line empiric therapy for acute uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women.

options.label: D
options.text: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM once, then oral cefixime
options.explanation: Parenteral therapy is unnecessary for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection.

options.label: E
options.text: Withhold antibiotics until urine culture results
options.explanation: With typical symptoms and a positive dipstick, empiric treatment is appropriate; culture is not routinely required in uncomplicated cases.

questions.explanation: Acute uncomplicated cystitis in a healthy, non-pregnant woman without systemic features is treated empirically. Nitrofurantoin (5 days), TMP-SMX (3 days, if local resistance is low) or fosfomycin (single dose) are first-line choices. Fever, flank pain or CVA tenderness would suggest pyelonephritis and change management.

questions.stem:
A 67-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history is found to have a sodium of 124 mmol/L on routine bloodwork. He is asymptomatic. He takes no medications. A chest radiograph done last week showed a right hilar mass.

He appears euvolemic: no orthostasis, normal jugular venous pressure, moist mucous membranes, no edema.

Serum osmolality: 258 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality: 480 mOsm/kg
Urine sodium: 52 mmol/L
TSH and morning cortisol: normal
Creatinine: 68 µmol/L
questions.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: A
options.explanation: First-line treatment for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic hyponatremia due to SIADH.

options.label: B
options.explanation: In SIADH the kidney excretes the sodium and retains the water, which can worsen hyponatremia when urine osmolality is high.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Reserved for severe symptoms such as seizures or decreased level of consciousness.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Loop diuretics are sometimes added to salt tablets in refractory SIADH, not used alone as initial therapy.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Thiazides cause or worsen hyponatremia.

questions.explanation: Hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm > 100), high urine sodium, clinical euvolemia, and normal thyroid, adrenal and renal function fits SIADH, here likely paraneoplastic from small cell lung cancer. Asymptomatic chronic SIADH is treated first with fluid restriction. Correct slowly (generally no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours) to avoid osmotic demyelination.

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presents with 2 days of vomiting and abdominal pain after running out of insulin. He is drowsy but oriented.

BP 104/62 mmHg, HR 118/min, RR 28/min with deep respirations.

Glucose: 31 mmol/L
Venous pH: 7.10
Bicarbonate: 8 mmol/L
Anion gap: 26
Potassium: 3.0 mmol/L
Serum β-hydroxybutyrate: elevated

A 1 L bolus of 0.9% saline has been started.
questions.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Start an IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h
options.explanation: Insulin shifts potassium into cells and can precipitate dangerous hypokalemia when K is below 3.3 mmol/L.

options.label: B
options.text: Give IV potassium chloride and hold insulin until potassium is at least 3.3 mmol/L
options.explanation: Correct: potassium must be repleted before insulin when the initial value is low.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Not indicated unless pH is below about 6.9 to 7.0, and it can worsen hypokalemia.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Any insulin before potassium repletion carries the same risk of life-threatening hypokalemia.

options.label: E
options.text: Give IV potassium phosphate as the sole electrolyte replacement
options.explanation: Routine phosphate replacement is not recommended; potassium chloride is the priority.

questions.explanation: Total body potassium is depleted in DKA even when serum levels are normal or high. With an initial K below 3.3 mmol/L, insulin is held while potassium is replaced, because insulin drives potassium intracellularly and can cause arrhythmias. Fluids continue in parallel. Once K is at least 3.3, start the insulin infusion and continue potassium in the fluids to keep it in the 4 to 5 range.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with two episodes of hematemesis and black, tarry stools since this morning. He takes naproxen daily for knee osteoarthritis.

He is pale and diaphoretic. BP 86/52 mmHg, HR 124/min. Abdomen is soft and non-tender. Hemoglobin is 82 g/L.
questions.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Endoscopy should follow, ideally within 24 hours, but an unstable patient is resuscitated first.

options.label: B
options.text: Two large-bore IV lines and fluid resuscitation, with blood products as needed
options.explanation: Correct: hemodynamic resuscitation takes priority in an unstable upper GI bleed.

options.label: C
options.explanation: IV PPI is reasonable before endoscopy, but oral therapy does not address shock and is not the first priority.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Considered for ongoing bleeding when endoscopy fails or the source is not found.

options.label: E
options.explanation: A rescue option for refractory variceal bleeding; nothing here suggests portal hypertension.

questions.explanation: This patient is in hemorrhagic shock from a likely NSAID-related peptic ulcer bleed. The first priority is resuscitation: large-bore IV access, crystalloid, and blood transfusion. A restrictive hemoglobin threshold of about 70 g/L applies to hemodynamically stable patients; in shock, transfusion is guided by ongoing bleeding and hemodynamics rather than a number. IV PPI is started and endoscopy performed after stabilization, ideally within 24 hours.

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old man is on postoperative day 8 after a total knee arthroplasty. He has been receiving subcutaneous unfractionated heparin for thromboprophylaxis since surgery. Today his calf is swollen and tender, and compression ultrasound shows a new popliteal vein thrombosis.

Platelets: 245 × 10⁹/L preoperatively, 230 × 10⁹/L on day 2, 98 × 10⁹/L today.
He has no bleeding and takes no other new medications.
questions.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Continuing heparin perpetuates HIT, and platelet transfusion is generally avoided absent bleeding.

options.label: B
options.explanation: LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies and is contraindicated.

options.label: C
options.text: Stop heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban
options.explanation: Correct: HIT is a prothrombotic state requiring therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulation.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop heparin and start warfarin immediately
options.explanation: Warfarin started during acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene through protein C depletion; it is started only after platelets recover, overlapped with a non-heparin agent.

options.label: E
options.text: Stop heparin and observe without anticoagulation
options.explanation: HIT carries a high thrombosis risk, and this patient already has a DVT.

questions.explanation: A platelet fall of more than 50% beginning 5 to 10 days after heparin exposure, with new thrombosis and no other cause, gives a high 4Ts score for HIT. Stop all heparin (including flushes) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, fondaparinux, or in selected stable patients a DOAC, while sending an HIT immunoassay. Avoid warfarin until the platelet count has recovered.
